Question four. Why is cache invalidation hard? Because there are two copies of the truth, and they drift. Set the TTL, the time to live, too long and users see stale data; too short and you lose the cache's benefit. The page models a key read about once a second and changed every two minutes. The least bad TTL is where the two failures cross, about fifteen seconds, and even there six percent of reads miss and six percent are stale. A short link barely changes, so its TTL can be long, until one is taken down for abuse. Then delete its cached entry after the database commits. Delete it first, and a read in between puts the old value back. The TTL stays as a backstop. Write-through updates both together, consistent at a cost on every write. Write-behind batches writes for speed, and a crash loses what it hadn't written.

Question five. What is database replication, and what does it buy you? Copies of the data on several nodes. In leader-follower replication, writes go to the leader and stream to read-only followers. That scales reads, and if the leader dies, a follower is promoted. The catch is replication lag. Someone creates a link and opens it at once, and the read lands on a follower that hasn't caught up: not found. So for a short while after a user writes, send their reads to the leader. And with asynchronous replication, promoting a lagging follower loses the writes it never received.
